name: Barbell Bench Press
description: The benchmark horizontal press and the most direct way to load the chest heavily.
instructions: Lie flat with your eyes under the bar, feet planted, and shoulder blades pulled back and down into the bench.
Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width and unrack to a position directly over your shoulders.
Lower the bar under control to the lower chest, keeping the elbows at roughly 45 degrees to the torso.
Press back up and slightly toward the face, finishing with the arms locked over the shoulder joint.

name: Barbell Back Squat
description: The foundational lower-body compound lift for building leg size and whole-body strength.
instructions: Rest the bar across your upper traps, not your neck, and pull your elbows down to lock your upper back tight.
Unrack, take two controlled steps back, and set your feet shoulder-width with the toes turned out slightly.
Brace hard, then break at the hips and knees together until the hip crease drops below the knee.
Drive through the whole foot and extend hips and knees at the same rate to stand tall.

name: Conventional Deadlift
description: A full-body pull from the floor that loads the entire posterior chain harder than anything else.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width and the bar directly over your mid-foot, roughly an inch from your shins.
Hinge down and take a grip just outside your knees, then drop the hips and lift the chest.
Pull the slack out of the bar, brace, and push the floor away rather than yanking the bar up.
Keep the bar in contact with your legs the whole way and finish by locking the hips and knees together.

name: Bodyweight Pull-Up
description: The benchmark vertical pull. Builds lat width, pulling strength and grip at the same time.
instructions: Take an overhand grip slightly wider than your shoulders and hang with the arms fully straight.
Set the shoulders down and back before you pull, so the lats take the load instead of the arms.
Drive the elbows down toward your ribs until your chin clears the bar.
Lower under control all the way back to a dead hang before starting the next rep.

name: Standing Dumbbell Shoulder Press
description: Builds deltoid mass while forcing the core to stabilise an overhead load.
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width and hold the dumbbells at shoulder height, palms facing forward.
Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs so the lower back does not arch as you press.
Press the dumbbells overhead until the arms are locked out and the weights are over the shoulders.
Lower under control back to shoulder level without letting the elbows drop below the wrists.

name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
description: A hip hinge that loads the hamstrings through a long, controlled stretch.
instructions: Hold the dumbbells in front of your thighs with a soft, unlocked bend in the knees.
Push your hips straight back and let the dumbbells travel down along the front of your legs.
Stop when you feel the hamstrings reach the end of their range with a flat back.
Drive the hips forward and squeeze the glutes to return upright.

name: Bodyweight Push-Up
description: The most portable horizontal press there is, and a genuine core exercise when done strictly.
instructions: Set your hands slightly wider than your shoulders with the body in one straight line from heels to head.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the abs so the hips neither sag nor pike up.
Lower until your chest is an inch off the floor, keeping the elbows at about 45 degrees.
Push the floor away to full lockout, letting the shoulder blades spread at the top.

name: Kettlebell Goblet Squat
description: The best squat-pattern teacher there is: the front load forces an upright torso automatically.
instructions: Hold the kettlebell by the horns against your upper chest with the elbows tucked in.
Set your feet slightly wider than your hips with the toes turned out a little.
Squat down by sending the hips back and letting the elbows pass inside the knees.
Drive through the whole foot to stand, keeping the weight pinned to your chest throughout.

name: Incline Dumbbell Biceps Curl
description: Isolates the long head of the biceps by starting every rep from a deep stretch.
instructions: Set an incline bench to roughly 45 degrees and sit back with a dumbbell in each hand.
Let the arms hang straight down behind the line of your torso so the biceps are stretched.
Curl the weights up without letting the elbows drift forward.
Lower slowly all the way back to the stretched position before the next rep.

name: Hanging Knee Raise
description: A hanging core drill that trains the abs to flex the spine rather than just hold it still.
instructions: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip and let the body settle without swinging.
Tilt the pelvis back first, then raise the knees toward your chest.
Squeeze the abs hard at the top rather than stopping once the hips reach 90 degrees.
Lower the legs slowly back to the hang, keeping the upper body still.

name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
description: Tilts the press to bias the clavicular head of the chest and the front delts.
instructions: Set the bench to about 30 degrees; steeper than that and it becomes a shoulder press.
Retract the shoulder blades into the pad and unrack the bar over your shoulders.
Lower the bar to the upper chest, just below the collarbone, with elbows tucked to 45 degrees.
Press back up along the same path without letting the shoulders roll forward at lockout.

name: Barbell Decline Bench Press
description: A shorter range press that shifts the load onto the lower chest and spares the shoulders.
instructions: Lock your legs into the decline bench and have a partner hand you the bar if it is heavy.
Take a grip slightly wider than shoulder-width with the shoulder blades pinned back.
Lower the bar to the lower chest, keeping the elbows from flaring past 45 degrees.
Press straight up and stop just short of locking the elbows to keep the chest under tension.

name: Dumbbell Bench Press
description: Allows a deeper stretch than the barbell and forces each side to work independently.
instructions: Sit on the end of the bench with the dumbbells on your thighs, then kick them back as you lie down.
Start with the dumbbells over your shoulders, palms facing forward, shoulder blades pinned.
Lower until the dumbbells are level with your chest and you feel a stretch across the pecs.
Press up and slightly inward, stopping just before the dumbbells clash at the top.

name: Incline Dumbbell Press
description: The most reliable upper-chest builder, with a longer range of motion than the barbell version.
instructions: Set the bench to roughly 30 degrees and sit back with a dumbbell resting on each thigh.
Kick the weights into position over your shoulders and pin the shoulder blades to the pad.
Lower the dumbbells to the sides of your upper chest until you feel a deep stretch.
Press up and together without letting the elbows flare straight out to the sides.

name: Flat Dumbbell Fly
description: An isolation movement that trains the chest through its stretched position with no triceps help.
instructions: Lie flat holding the dumbbells over your chest with the palms facing each other.
Keep a fixed, slightly bent elbow angle for the whole set -- this is not a press.
Open the arms out in a wide arc until the chest is stretched, stopping level with the torso.
Squeeze the chest to bring the dumbbells back together along the same arc.

name: Incline Dumbbell Fly
description: Isolates the upper chest at full stretch, where the fly does most of its work.
instructions: Set the bench to about 30 degrees and start with the dumbbells over your chest, palms facing in.
Lock in a soft bend at the elbows and hold that angle throughout the set.
Lower the arms out and down in a wide arc until you feel a strong stretch across the upper chest.
Bring the dumbbells back together by squeezing the pecs, not by pressing with the arms.

name: Dumbbell Pull-Over
description: An old-school movement that hits the chest or the lats depending on how you set your elbows.
instructions: Lie along or across a flat bench and hold a single dumbbell over your chest with both hands.
Flare the elbows wide to target the chest, or keep them tucked in to target the lats.
Lower the weight back over your head until you feel a stretch through the ribcage.
Pull the dumbbell back over your chest without letting the lower back arch off the bench.

name: Dumbbell Floor Press
description: A shortened-range press that spares the shoulders and shifts emphasis onto the lockout.
instructions: Lie on the floor with knees bent and the dumbbells held over your shoulders.
Lower until the backs of your upper arms touch the floor, elbows tucked to 45 degrees.
Pause for a beat so the floor kills any bounce out of the bottom.
Press back up powerfully to full lockout over the shoulders.

name: Landmine Chest Press
description: A standing press on an arc that hits the upper and middle chest with almost no shoulder strain.
instructions: Load one end of a barbell into a landmine and cup the sleeve with both hands at chest height.
Stand in a staggered stance with the core braced and the elbows tucked in close.
Press the bar up and away from you along its natural arc until the arms are extended.
Return under control to the chest without letting the torso lean back.

name: Plate Press
description: A constant-tension squeeze press that lights up the inner chest with very little equipment.
instructions: Hold a single weight plate between your palms at chest height, arms bent.
Squeeze the plate hard between your hands and keep squeezing for the whole set.
Press the plate straight out in front of you until the arms are extended.
Draw it back to the chest slowly, never releasing the inward pressure.

name: Swiss Ball Dumbbell Chest Press
description: A pressing variation that adds a heavy stability demand on the core and glutes.
instructions: Walk out on the ball until your upper back and head are supported and your hips are up.
Hold the dumbbells over your chest and squeeze the glutes to keep the torso level.
Lower the weights to chest level under tight control -- go lighter than your bench weight.
Press back up without letting the hips drop or the ball roll underneath you.

name: Incline Swiss Ball Dumbbell Chest Press
description: Uses the ball to create a decline-to-incline angle while the core fights to hold position.
instructions: Sit on the ball and walk your feet out until your lower back is supported and your torso is inclined.
Hold the dumbbells at the sides of your upper chest with the shoulder blades pulled back.
Press the weights up and slightly together, keeping the hips locked in place.
Lower under control to the stretch position without letting the ball shift.

name: Low-To-High Cable Fly
description: Sweeps the arms upward against the cable line to load the upper chest with constant tension.
instructions: Set both pulleys to the lowest setting and take a handle in each hand with a staggered stance.
Start with the arms down at your sides and a fixed soft bend in the elbows.
Sweep the hands up and together until they meet around chin height, squeezing the upper chest.
Resist the cables on the way back down until you feel a stretch across the front of the chest.

name: High-To-Low Cable Fly
description: Pulls down and across the body to bias the lower chest fibres through a full contraction.
instructions: Set both pulleys high, grab a handle in each hand and step forward into a split stance.
Hold a slight forward lean with the elbows softly bent and locked at that angle.
Sweep the hands down and together in front of your hips, crossing slightly at the finish.
Let the cables draw the arms back up and out until the chest is fully stretched.

name: Middle Cable Chest Fly
description: The neutral cable fly angle, hitting the mid-chest with even tension end to end.
instructions: Set both pulleys to roughly chest height and take a handle in each hand.
Step forward into a staggered stance with the arms out wide and elbows softly bent.
Bring the handles together in front of your sternum and hold the squeeze for a beat.
Open the arms back out slowly until you feel the stretch, keeping the elbow angle fixed.

name: Low Cable Chest Fly
description: A low-pulley fly that keeps the upper chest loaded hardest at the top of the rep.
instructions: Drop both pulleys to the bottom and take a handle in each hand, palms facing forward.
Step forward with a slight forward torso lean and soft elbows.
Sweep the arms up and in toward the centre of your chest.
Lower slowly back out and down, keeping the cables under tension the whole way.

name: High Cable Chest Fly
description: A downward fly arc that finishes with a hard lower-chest contraction in front of the hips.
instructions: Set both pulleys above head height and grab a handle in each hand.
Step forward, lean in slightly, and start with the arms out wide and high.
Pull the handles down and together in front of your waist, squeezing at the bottom.
Let the arms travel back up and out under control to a full stretch.

name: Smith Machine Bench Press
description: A fixed bar path press, useful for training close to failure without a spotter.
instructions: Position the bench so the bar lines up with your lower chest when it comes down.
Set your grip slightly wider than shoulder-width and twist the bar to unhook it.
Lower to the chest under control with the elbows at roughly 45 degrees.
Press up to lockout, and rotate the bar back into the hooks to finish the set.

name: Smith Machine Incline Bench Press
description: Upper-chest pressing on rails, so all your attention goes into the contraction.
instructions: Set an incline bench under the bar at about 30 degrees and line the bar up with your upper chest.
Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width and unhook the bar.
Lower the bar to just below the collarbone, keeping the shoulder blades pinned back.
Press up to full extension without letting the shoulders shrug forward.

name: Incline Chest Press Machine
description: Plate-loaded upper-chest pressing with independent arms and zero balance demand.
instructions: Adjust the seat so the handles sit level with your upper chest when you grip them.
Sit back with the shoulder blades pulled down into the pad and feet flat on the floor.
Press the handles up and forward until the arms are almost locked out.
Return slowly until you feel the stretch, stopping before the weight stack touches down.

name: Seated Chest Press Machine
description: The simplest way to load the chest heavily -- a good first pressing movement for beginners.
instructions: Set the seat height so the handles line up with the middle of your chest.
Sit tall with your back flat against the pad and grip the handles.
Press forward until the arms are extended but not locked hard.
Let the handles come back slowly until your hands are level with your chest.

name: Chest Dip
description: A heavy bodyweight press. Leaning forward turns the dip from a triceps move into a chest move.
instructions: Support yourself on parallel bars with the arms locked out and the shoulders down.
Lean the torso forward and let the elbows travel out slightly -- this is what targets the chest.
Lower until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor and you feel the chest stretch.
Press back to lockout, keeping the forward lean the whole way up.

name: Weighted Dip
description: The progression once bodyweight dips stop being challenging.
instructions: Hang a plate or dumbbell from a dip belt, or hold a dumbbell between your feet.
Get into the top position with the arms locked and the shoulders pulled down away from the ears.
Lower under strict control to a stretch, never letting the shoulders roll forward.
Press back up to lockout and keep the extra load steady so it does not swing.

name: Decline Push-Up
description: Elevating the feet shifts more bodyweight onto the upper chest and front delts.
instructions: Place your feet up on a bench or box with the hands slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hold a straight line from heels to head with the glutes and abs braced.
Lower until the chest is just off the floor, keeping the elbows at about 45 degrees.
Press back up to full lockout without letting the hips sag.

name: Explosive Plyo Push-Up
description: A power push-up that trains rate of force development in the pressing muscles.
instructions: Start in a standard push-up position with the core braced hard.
Lower quickly but under control to just above the floor.
Drive up explosively so the hands leave the ground at the top.
Land with soft elbows and absorb the impact straight into the next rep.

name: Knuckle Push-Up
description: A push-up on the knuckles that adds depth and keeps the wrists in a neutral position.
instructions: Make fists and set your knuckles on a mat, shoulder-width apart, wrists straight.
Hold a rigid plank from heels to head.
Lower deeper than a normal push-up, using the extra height the fists give you.
Press back up without letting the wrists bend or the fists roll outward.

name: Judo Push-Up
description: A flowing push-up that sweeps from a pike into a cobra, loading chest and shoulders together.
instructions: Start with the hips high in a downward-dog position, hands shoulder-width apart.
Dive the chest forward and down, passing close to the floor as if going under a bar.
Finish by pressing the chest up with the hips low and the arms extended.
Reverse the movement back to the pike position to complete the rep.

name: Medicine Ball Push-Up
description: A narrow, unstable push-up that hits the inner chest and triceps hard.
instructions: Place both hands on top of a medicine ball directly under your chest.
Set a rigid plank with the glutes squeezed and the ball held still.
Lower your chest to the ball, keeping the elbows brushing past your ribs.
Press back up to lockout without letting the ball roll away from you.

name: Single-Arm Medicine Ball Push-Up
description: An offset push-up where one hand is elevated, forcing the core to fight rotation.
instructions: Set one hand on a medicine ball and the other flat on the floor, slightly wider than the shoulder.
Brace hard so the hips stay square rather than twisting toward the low side.
Lower until the chest is level with the ball hand.
Press up evenly and swap sides after each set.

name: Swiss Ball Push-Up
description: A push-up with the hands on a ball, turning it into a serious anti-wobble core exercise.
instructions: Place both hands on the sides of an exercise ball and walk the feet back into a plank.
Squeeze the ball inward slightly to steady it before you start.
Lower your chest toward the ball with the elbows tucked in.
Press back up smoothly, keeping the ball from rocking side to side.

name: Feet-Elevated Exercise Ball Push-Up
description: Feet on the ball, hands on the floor -- a decline push-up with a punishing core demand.
instructions: Set your shins or feet on top of an exercise ball with your hands under your shoulders.
Brace the abs and glutes so the hips do not sag or the ball roll.
Lower your chest toward the floor with the elbows at about 45 degrees.
Press back up in a straight line, keeping the ball completely still.

name: Dumbbell T Push-Up
description: A push-up plus a rotation into a side plank, combining pressing with anti-rotation work.
instructions: Start in a push-up position gripping a dumbbell in each hand, wrists locked straight.
Perform a full push-up with the elbows tucked toward your ribs.
At the top, rotate onto one side and raise that dumbbell straight up into a T position.
Come back down under control and alternate sides on every rep.

name: Dumbbell Push-Up Into Row
description: Pairs a push and a pull in one rep while the core resists rotation throughout.
instructions: Get into a push-up position holding a hex dumbbell in each hand, feet spread wide for balance.
Complete one strict push-up, keeping the wrists stacked over the dumbbells.
At the top, row one dumbbell to your ribs without letting the hips twist.
Lower it, row the other side, then go straight into the next push-up.

name: Barbell Bent-Over Row
description: The heaviest horizontal pull you can train, and the backbone of most back routines.
instructions: Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is around 45 degrees, knees softly bent.
Hold the bar with an overhand grip just outside shoulder-width and let it hang at arm's length.
Pull the bar into your lower ribs by driving the elbows back, keeping the back flat.
Lower under control to a full stretch without letting the torso rise up to help.

name: Pendlay Row
description: A dead-stop row from the floor. Every rep starts from zero, so momentum cannot help you.
instructions: Set the bar on the floor and hinge over until your torso is parallel to the ground.
Take an overhand grip outside the knees and brace the whole midsection.
Explode the bar up into your lower chest without raising the torso at all.
Return the bar all the way to the floor and reset before the next rep.

name: Single-Arm Barbell Row
description: Rowing one side at a time gives a longer range of motion and exposes side-to-side imbalances.
instructions: Stand beside a loaded barbell in a landmine or corner and hinge over, one hand braced on your thigh.
Grip the bar with the free hand and let it hang in a full stretch.
Row the bar back toward your hip, driving the elbow past the ribs.
Lower slowly, letting the shoulder blade travel forward at the bottom, then repeat.

name: Dumbbell Bent-Over Row
description: A two-dumbbell row that lets each arm move freely and is easier on the lower back than a barbell.
instructions: Hinge at the hips with a flat back until the torso is around 45 degrees, dumbbells hanging down.
Set the shoulder blades and brace the core before the first rep.
Pull both dumbbells to your ribs, leading with the elbows rather than the hands.
Lower them all the way down to a full stretch under control.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
description: Braced on a bench, this is the most controlled way to train the lats one side at a time.
instructions: Put one knee and the same-side hand on a bench with the spine neutral and hips square.
Hold the dumbbell in the free hand at arm's length, letting the shoulder blade stretch forward.
Drive the elbow toward your hip until the dumbbell reaches the side of your ribs.
Lower slowly back to the stretch without rotating the torso to chase extra range.

name: Single-Leg Neutral-Grip Dumbbell Row
description: A row balanced on one leg, adding a serious posterior-chain and balance challenge.
instructions: Hinge forward on one leg with the other leg extended straight behind you for counterbalance.
Hold a dumbbell in the opposite hand, hanging directly below your shoulder.
Row the dumbbell to your hip while keeping the hips level and square to the floor.
Lower under control and complete all reps before switching sides.

name: T-Bar Row
description: A supported row angle that lets you use heavy weight with a neutral grip and thick-back emphasis.
instructions: Straddle the loaded bar and grip the handle with the chest up and knees bent.
Hinge forward until the torso is about 45 degrees and brace the lower back hard.
Pull the handle into your stomach, squeezing the shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower to a full stretch without rounding the back or bouncing the plates.

name: Strap Bent-Over Row
description: A bodyweight row on suspension straps -- scale the difficulty just by moving your feet.
instructions: Grab the handles and walk your feet forward so your body is leaning back at an angle.
Hold a rigid plank from heels to head with the arms fully extended.
Pull your chest to your hands, driving the elbows back and squeezing the shoulder blades.
Lower under control to a full stretch; step your feet further forward to make it harder.

name: Smith Machine Bent-Over Row
description: The fixed bar path takes balance out of the row so you can focus entirely on the pull.
instructions: Set the bar just below knee height and take an overhand grip outside shoulder-width.
Hinge over with a flat back, unhook the bar and let it hang at arm's length.
Row the bar to your lower ribs by driving the elbows back and up.
Lower to a dead stretch, keeping the torso angle fixed the whole set.

name: Inverted Row
description: The horizontal counterpart to the push-up and the best entry point into pulling strength.
instructions: Set a bar at roughly hip height and lie underneath it with an overhand grip.
Hang with the arms straight and the body in one rigid line from heels to head.
Pull your chest up to the bar, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Lower under control to full arm extension without letting the hips drop first.

name: Feet-Elevated Inverted Row
description: Raising the feet to bar height makes the inverted row close to a full bodyweight pull.
instructions: Set the bar at hip height and put your feet up on a bench so the body is horizontal.
Take an overhand grip slightly wider than your shoulders and hang with straight arms.
Pull the chest to the bar while keeping the glutes squeezed and the body flat.
Lower slowly to full extension and reset the shoulder blades before the next rep.

name: Lat Pulldown
description: A scalable vertical pull and the most direct route to building the strength for pull-ups.
instructions: Lock your thighs under the pad and take an overhand grip a little wider than your shoulders.
Lean back only slightly and pull the shoulders down before the elbows move.
Drive the elbows down to bring the bar to your upper chest.
Let the bar rise back up until the lats are fully stretched and the shoulders lift.

name: Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldown
description: An underhand pulldown that shortens the arm path and brings the biceps and lower lats in harder.
instructions: Take a shoulder-width underhand grip on the bar and lock your thighs under the pad.
Keep the chest up and lean back just a few degrees.
Pull the bar down to the top of your chest, driving the elbows toward your hips.
Control the bar all the way back up to a full stretch overhead.

name: Single-Arm Reverse Pulldown
description: A one-armed pulldown that lets the lat travel through its full range without the other side compensating.
instructions: Attach a single handle to the high pulley and take it with an underhand grip.
Kneel or sit with the torso tall and the working shoulder stretched up toward the pulley.
Pull the handle down to the side of your chest, driving the elbow toward your hip.
Let the arm extend fully overhead again, allowing the shoulder blade to rise.

name: Strap Lat Pulldown
description: Using straps instead of a bar takes the grip and biceps out so the lats do all the work.
instructions: Clip a pair of straps or single handles to the high pulley and take one in each hand.
Sit with your thighs locked under the pad and the arms stretched overhead.
Pull the hands down and out to the sides, thinking about driving the elbows into your pockets.
Let the arms travel back overhead under control until the lats are stretched again.

name: Seated Cable Row
description: The staple horizontal cable pull, with tension held evenly from stretch to contraction.
instructions: Sit with your feet on the platform and a slight bend in the knees, chest up.
Reach forward to grab the handle and let the shoulder blades travel forward at the stretch.
Pull the handle to your stomach, driving the elbows back and squeezing the blades together.
Return to the stretch slowly, keeping the torso upright rather than rocking back and forth.

name: Wide-Grip Cable Low Row
description: A wide-grip row that pulls the elbows out and away, targeting the upper back rather than the lats.
instructions: Attach a wide bar to the low pulley and sit with the chest tall and knees softly bent.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip.
Pull the bar to the top of your stomach with the elbows flared out to the sides.
Let the bar travel back out until the upper back is fully stretched.

name: Strap Low Row
description: A neutral-grip cable row using straps, so the wrists stay comfortable and the back does the work.
instructions: Clip straps or a pair of handles to the low pulley and sit facing the machine.
Extend the arms forward and let the shoulder blades stretch out.
Row both hands to your sides, keeping the elbows tight to the ribs.
Return slowly to the stretch, resisting the pull the whole way.

name: Standing Lat Pushdown
description: A straight-arm pushdown that isolates the lats without any elbow bend or biceps involvement.
instructions: Stand facing a high pulley with a straight bar, hands about shoulder-width apart.
Hinge forward slightly and lock the elbows at a fixed, near-straight angle.
Push the bar down in an arc until it reaches the front of your thighs.
Let the bar rise back up until you feel the lats stretch, without bending the elbows.

name: Seated Lat Pulldown Machine
description: Plate-loaded pulldown with independent arms, useful for evening out a strength difference.
instructions: Set the seat and thigh pad so you are locked in with the arms fully extended overhead.
Take the handles with a neutral or overhand grip and set the chest tall.
Pull the handles down to shoulder height by driving the elbows down.
Let the arms extend fully overhead again before starting the next rep.

name: Beginner Pull-Up
description: Assisted and negative pull-up progressions for building up to your first strict rep.
instructions: Set a box or bench under the bar so you can step up into the top position.
Start with your chin over the bar and the shoulders pulled down and back.
Lower yourself as slowly as you can -- aim for three to five seconds per rep.
Step back up and repeat; once you can control a five-second negative, start attempting full reps.

name: Weighted Pull-Up
description: The progression once you can do clean bodyweight sets -- the simplest way to keep overloading a pull-up.
instructions: Attach a plate to a dip belt or hold a dumbbell between your feet.
Hang with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder-width, shoulders set down.
Pull until the chin clears the bar, keeping the extra load from swinging.
Lower under full control back to a dead hang.

name: Weighted Chin-Up
description: The underhand grip lets you handle more load and pulls the biceps in as a major mover.
instructions: Load a dip belt and take a shoulder-width underhand grip on the bar.
Hang with the arms straight and the shoulders pulled down away from your ears.
Pull your chest toward the bar, driving the elbows down toward your ribs.
Lower slowly to a dead hang, keeping the added weight steady.

name: Strap Chin-Up
description: Chin-ups on straps let the wrists rotate freely, which is easier on the elbows than a fixed bar.
instructions: Hang from a pair of straps or rings with the palms facing each other.
Set the shoulders down and back before you begin the pull.
Pull up, rotating the palms to face you as you rise, until the chin clears your hands.
Lower back to a full hang, letting the hands rotate back to neutral.

name: Tennis Ball Pull-Up
description: Pull-ups gripping tennis balls -- a brutal grip and forearm builder used by climbers.
instructions: Fix a tennis ball over each end of your grip position, or hold one in each hand over the bar.
Take a firm grip and hang with the shoulders set.
Pull up as normal, fighting to keep the balls from slipping.
Lower under control and expect far fewer reps than a standard pull-up.

name: Ring Muscle-Up
description: A pull-up and a dip joined by a transition -- one of the hardest bodyweight movements there is.
instructions: Hang from the rings with a false grip, wrists resting over the top of the rings.
Pull explosively, keeping the rings tight to your body rather than out in front.
As your chest reaches ring height, drive the elbows back and roll the wrists over into the dip.
Press out to lockout, then reverse the whole sequence back down to the hang.

name: Monkey Pull
description: An alternating single-arm cable pull that keeps one side under tension while the other works.
instructions: Set two high pulleys and take a handle in each hand, stepping back into a braced stance.
Start with both arms extended overhead, torso leaning back slightly.
Pull one handle down to your ribs while the other stays extended.
Alternate sides continuously, keeping constant tension on both cables.

name: Barbell Shrug
description: The most straightforward trap builder -- straight up, straight down, no rolling.
instructions: Hold the bar in front of your thighs with an overhand grip just outside your hips.
Stand tall with the chest up and the arms completely straight.
Shrug the shoulders straight up toward your ears and hold the squeeze for a beat.
Lower under control to a full stretch -- never roll the shoulders backward.

name: Wide-Grip Barbell Shrug
description: Widening the grip shifts the shrug toward the upper back rather than just the top of the traps.
instructions: Take a grip well outside shoulder-width with the bar hanging in front of your thighs.
Stand tall, chest up, arms straight and relaxed at the elbow.
Shrug straight up, thinking about pulling the outer traps toward the ceiling.
Lower slowly to a full stretch before the next rep.

name: Dumbbell Shrug
description: Dumbbells at your sides let the traps work through a slightly longer range than a barbell.
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand hanging at your sides, palms facing in.
Keep the arms straight and the chin level throughout.
Shrug the shoulders straight up as high as you can and pause at the top.
Lower all the way down until you feel the traps stretch.

name: Front Dumbbell Shrug
description: Holding the dumbbells in front of the thighs changes the line of pull on the traps.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs with the palms facing your body.
Stand tall with the arms straight and the shoulders relaxed down.
Shrug straight up toward the ears without letting the dumbbells swing forward.
Lower under control to a full stretch.

name: Smith Machine Reverse Shrug
description: Shrugging with the bar behind you biases the mid-traps and helps pull the shoulders back.
instructions: Stand with your back to the Smith bar and grip it behind your glutes, overhand.
Unhook the bar and stand tall with the chest up and arms straight.
Shrug the shoulders straight up, feeling the squeeze between the shoulder blades.
Lower slowly and keep the bar close to your body throughout.

name: Superman Hyperextension
description: Direct lower-back work on the hyperextension bench, with the arms extended to add leverage.
instructions: Set the pad just below your hip bones so you can hinge freely.
Cross the arms over your chest or extend them overhead for extra difficulty.
Lower your torso by hinging at the hips until you feel the hamstrings and lower back stretch.
Raise back up until your body is straight -- do not arch past neutral at the top.

name: Alternating Superman
description: A floor drill for the spinal erectors and glutes that needs no equipment at all.
instructions: Lie face down with the arms extended overhead and the legs straight.
Raise one arm and the opposite leg a few inches off the floor.
Hold the top position for a beat, keeping the neck in line with the spine.
Lower and switch to the other side, alternating for the whole set.

name: Rack Pull
description: A partial deadlift from pins that overloads the top half and builds a thicker upper back.
instructions: Set the safety pins so the bar starts at or just below knee height.
Take your normal deadlift stance and grip, with the shins close to the bar.
Brace, pull the slack out, and drive the hips forward to lock the bar out.
Lower back to the pins under control rather than dropping it.

name: Deficit Deadlift
description: Pulling from a raised platform lengthens the range of motion and strengthens the bottom of the deadlift.
instructions: Stand on a plate or platform one to two inches high with the bar over your mid-foot.
Hinge down and grip the bar -- expect the hips to sit lower than a normal deadlift.
Brace hard, keep the chest up, and push the floor away.
Use noticeably less weight than your regular deadlift and stop the set if the back rounds.

name: Sumo Deadlift
description: A wide-stance deadlift with a shorter range of motion and a far more upright torso.
instructions: Take a wide stance with the toes turned out and the shins close to the bar.
Grip inside your knees, drop the hips and lift the chest so the back is flat.
Push the knees out over the toes and drive the floor apart as you stand.
Lock out the hips and knees together, then lower the bar under control.

name: Dumbbell Deadlift
description: A beginner-friendly hinge that teaches the deadlift pattern without needing a barbell.
instructions: Stand with feet hip-width and a dumbbell on the floor just outside each foot.
Hinge at the hips, bend the knees, and grip the dumbbells with a flat back.
Drive through the floor and stand tall, keeping the dumbbells close to your legs.
Push the hips back to lower the weights under control back to the floor.

name: Hip Hinge
description: The pattern drill behind every deadlift, row and RDL. Worth learning before you load any of them.
instructions: Hold a dowel or broomstick against your head, upper back and tailbone.
Push the hips straight back with a soft knee bend, letting the torso tip forward.
Keep all three contact points touching the stick the whole way down.
Drive the hips forward to stand tall, squeezing the glutes at the top.

name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
description: The strict military press. A true test of shoulder strength and full-body bracing.
instructions: Take the bar out of the rack onto your front delts with a grip just outside shoulder-width.
Squeeze the glutes and brace the abs so the lower back cannot arch.
Press the bar straight up, moving your head back slightly to clear a path.
Finish with the bar over your mid-foot and the biceps beside your ears, then lower under control.

name: Seated Barbell Shoulder Press
description: Sitting removes the leg drive so the delts carry the whole lift.
instructions: Set an upright bench inside a rack with the bar just above your head when seated.
Take a grip slightly wider than your shoulders and unrack to the front delts.
Press straight overhead without letting the lower back peel off the pad.
Lower under control until the bar is level with your chin.

name: Barbell Push Press
description: Adds leg drive to the overhead press so you can move more weight and train explosive power.
instructions: Start with the bar racked on the front delts, feet hip-width and core braced.
Dip by bending the knees a few inches with the torso staying vertical.
Reverse hard and use that drive to launch the bar off your shoulders.
Punch the arms to lockout overhead, then lower back to the shoulders and reset.

name: Overhead Press Machine
description: A guided overhead press, ideal for training the delts close to failure without a spotter.
instructions: Set the seat so the handles start level with your shoulders.
Sit tall with the back flat against the pad and grip the handles.
Press overhead until the arms are almost locked out.
Lower slowly back to shoulder height without letting the weight stack rest.

name: Squat To Alternating Dumbbell Press
description: A full-body combo that pairs a squat with an alternating overhead press.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell at each shoulder and stand with the feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down to depth, keeping the chest tall and the weights racked.
Stand up and press one dumbbell overhead as you reach the top.
Lower it, squat again, and press with the other arm -- alternate for the whole set.

name: Dumbbell Side Lateral Raise
description: The single best exercise for the side delts, which is what actually makes shoulders look wide.
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, elbows slightly bent.
Raise the arms out to the sides, leading with the elbows rather than the hands.
Stop at shoulder height -- going higher hands the work to the traps.
Lower slowly under control rather than letting the weights drop.

name: Lateral Raise For Shoulder Health
description: A light, high-rep lateral raise variation used to warm up or rehab cranky shoulders.
instructions: Use very light dumbbells -- this is a blood-flow drill, not a strength set.
Raise the arms out to the sides with the thumbs turned slightly upward.
Stop just below shoulder height and avoid any shrugging.
Perform high reps with a slow, smooth tempo throughout.

name: Dumbbell Front Raise
description: Isolates the front delts, useful if your pressing volume is low.
instructions: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, palms facing back.
Brace the core so the torso does not swing backward to help.
Raise one arm straight out in front to shoulder height with a soft elbow.
Lower under control and alternate arms, or raise both together.

name: Barbell Front Raise
description: A two-handed front raise that keeps both delts loading evenly.
instructions: Hold a barbell in front of your thighs with an overhand, shoulder-width grip.
Stand tall with the core braced and the knees softly bent.
Raise the bar straight out in front to shoulder height, arms nearly straight.
Lower slowly without leaning back or using the hips to swing the bar up.

name: Overhead Plate Raise
description: A front raise taken all the way overhead, hitting the front delts through a longer range.
instructions: Hold a weight plate at the sides, arms hanging down in front of your hips.
Brace the abs and squeeze the glutes so the ribs stay down.
Raise the plate in a wide arc all the way overhead with near-straight arms.
Lower it back down along the same path under control.

name: Dumbbell Bent-Over Rear Raise
description: The staple rear-delt movement, and the fix for shoulders that look flat from the side.
instructions: Hinge forward at the hips until the torso is close to parallel with the floor.
Let the dumbbells hang below your chest with a soft bend in the elbows.
Raise the arms out to the sides until they are level with your back.
Lower slowly, keeping the elbow angle fixed and the torso still.

name: Dumbbell Rear Fly
description: A rear fly variation set up so the delts stay loaded instead of the traps taking over.
instructions: Set an incline bench low and lie chest-down on it, or hinge over with the chest supported.
Let the dumbbells hang straight down with the palms facing each other.
Sweep the arms out and slightly back, thinking about pulling with the rear delts.
Pause at the top for a beat, then lower all the way back down.

name: Overhand-Grip Rear Lateral Raise
description: Pronating the grip rotates the shoulder so the rear delt is in its strongest pulling position.
instructions: Hinge forward with the dumbbells hanging below you, palms facing behind you.
Keep the elbows fixed at a soft bend for the whole set.
Raise the arms out to the sides with the thumbs pointing down toward the floor.
Stop level with your back, then lower under control.

name: Incline Single-Arm Rear Raise
description: Chest-supported and one arm at a time, so there is nowhere for momentum to hide.
instructions: Lie chest-down on a low incline bench with one dumbbell hanging toward the floor.
Set the shoulder blade down before the arm moves.
Raise the dumbbell out to the side until it is level with your torso.
Lower slowly to a full stretch, then finish the set before switching sides.

name: Incline Dumbbell W Raise
description: A rear-delt and mid-trap drill that pulls the arms into a W shape at the top.
instructions: Lie chest-down on a low incline bench with light dumbbells hanging below you.
Bend the elbows to about 90 degrees, palms facing down.
Pull the elbows back and up so the arms form a W, squeezing the shoulder blades.
Lower slowly back to the hang -- use light weight, this one exposes ego lifting fast.

name: Dumbbell Rear Raise Into Kickback
description: A combo rep that trains the rear delts and triceps back to back without putting the weights down.
instructions: Hinge forward with a dumbbell in each hand hanging below your chest.
Perform a rear raise, taking the arms out to the sides until level with your back.
Lower to the start, then tuck the elbows in and kick the dumbbells back behind you.
Return to the hang -- that is one rep of the pair.

name: Face Pull
description: The single most valuable prehab exercise for lifters -- it undoes what heavy pressing does to your shoulders.
instructions: Attach a rope to a pulley set slightly above head height and grip both ends overhand.
Step back until the cable is taut and hold the arms out straight.
Pull the rope toward your forehead, splitting the ends apart and driving the elbows high.
Squeeze for a beat with the hands beside your ears, then return under control.

name: Rear Delt Machine
description: A fixed-path reverse fly, the easiest way to train rear delts with strict form.
instructions: Set the seat so the handles are level with your shoulders and sit chest against the pad.
Grip the handles with a neutral or overhand grip and soft elbows.
Sweep the arms out and back until they are level with your torso.
Return slowly, resisting the weight all the way to the stretch.

name: Cable Shoulder Fly On Ball
description: A seated cable lateral raise on an exercise ball, adding a stability demand to the delt work.
instructions: Sit on an exercise ball between two low pulleys and take the opposite handle in each hand.
Start with the arms crossed in front of you and the cables under tension.
Raise the arms out to the sides to shoulder height, keeping the elbows soft.
Lower slowly back across the body without letting the ball roll.

name: Barbell Upright Row
description: A vertical pull for the side delts and traps. Use a wider grip if narrow feels pinchy.
instructions: Hold the bar in front of your thighs with an overhand grip about shoulder-width.
Stand tall with the chest up and the core braced.
Pull the bar straight up the front of your body, leading with the elbows.
Stop when the elbows reach shoulder height, then lower under control.

name: Dumbbell Upright Row
description: Dumbbells let the wrists find a natural path, which usually feels better than a straight bar.
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs.
Pull the weights straight up close to your body, driving the elbows out and up.
Stop when the elbows reach shoulder height, hands just below.
Lower under control back to the thighs.

name: Smith Machine Upright Row
description: The guided bar keeps the path perfectly vertical so the delts and traps do all the work.
instructions: Stand close to the Smith bar and grip it overhand at about shoulder-width.
Unhook the bar and stand tall with the arms straight.
Pull the bar up the front of your torso, keeping it close to your body.
Stop at chest height and lower slowly back down.

name: Arm Circles
description: A warm-up drill that takes the shoulder through its full range before you load it.
instructions: Stand tall with the arms extended straight out to your sides at shoulder height.
Draw small circles forward, gradually making them larger.
Reverse direction and repeat, starting large and working back down to small.
Keep the shoulders down away from the ears and the core braced throughout.

name: Barbell Curl
description: The heaviest biceps exercise you can load, and the benchmark for arm strength.
instructions: Stand tall holding the bar with an underhand, shoulder-width grip.
Pin the elbows to your sides and brace the core so the torso stays still.
Curl the bar up to chest height by bending only at the elbow.
Lower slowly all the way to straight arms -- the stretch is where the growth is.

name: Close-Grip Barbell Curl
description: Narrowing the grip shifts emphasis toward the outer, long head of the biceps.
instructions: Take an underhand grip on the bar with the hands roughly six inches apart.
Stand tall with the elbows tucked in tight against your ribs.
Curl the bar up without letting the elbows drift forward.
Lower under control to full arm extension.

name: Barbell Drag Curl
description: Dragging the bar up the body pulls the elbows back and hits the long head where the peak sits.
instructions: Hold the bar with a shoulder-width underhand grip resting against your thighs.
Instead of curling out, drag the bar straight up your torso.
Let the elbows travel backward behind your body as the bar rises.
Stop around the lower chest, then lower along the same path staying in contact with your body.

name: Reverse Barbell Curl
description: An overhand curl that builds the brachialis and forearm extensors -- it thickens the whole arm.
instructions: Grip the bar overhand at shoulder-width with the arms hanging straight.
Keep the elbows pinned to your sides and the wrists locked straight.
Curl the bar up, resisting the urge to let the wrists bend back.
Lower slowly -- expect to use noticeably less weight than a normal curl.

name: Close-Grip EZ-Bar Curl
description: The angled bar keeps the wrists comfortable while the narrow grip targets the outer biceps.
instructions: Take the inner angled sections of the EZ-bar with an underhand grip.
Stand tall with the elbows tight to your sides.
Curl the bar up to chest height without swinging the torso.
Lower under full control to straight arms.

name: Wide-Grip EZ-Bar Curl
description: The wide grip biases the short, inner head of the biceps.
instructions: Grip the outer angled sections of the EZ-bar with the palms up.
Set the elbows at your sides and keep the chest tall.
Curl the bar up while keeping the upper arms completely still.
Lower slowly all the way down before the next rep.

name: Inside-Grip EZ-Bar Curl
description: A narrow EZ-bar curl that keeps constant tension on the long head through the whole rep.
instructions: Take the innermost grip on the EZ-bar with the palms facing up.
Keep the elbows locked to your ribs and the shoulders down.
Curl the bar up in a tight arc, squeezing hard at the top.
Lower under control until the arms are fully straight.

name: Alternating Dumbbell Curl
description: One arm at a time, with supination built in so the biceps get their full contraction.
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing your thighs.
Curl one dumbbell up, rotating the palm to face the ceiling as you rise.
Squeeze at the top, then lower and rotate the palm back to neutral.
Alternate arms, keeping the non-working arm still rather than swinging it.

name: Dumbbell Hammer Curl
description: The neutral grip loads the brachialis, which sits under the biceps and pushes the peak up.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand with the palms facing your body.
Keep the elbows tight to your sides and the wrists locked straight.
Curl the weights up without rotating the palms at any point.
Lower under control to a full stretch at the bottom.

name: Dumbbell Side Curl
description: Curling out to the side changes the line of pull and hits the biceps from a fresh angle.
instructions: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, arms out slightly away from your body.
Keep the upper arms fixed and the palms facing forward.
Curl the weights up and out to the sides rather than straight in front.
Squeeze at the top, then lower under control.

name: Spider Curl
description: Chest-supported with the arms hanging free -- there is no way to cheat this one.
instructions: Lie chest-down on a bench set to about 45 degrees with the arms hanging straight down.
Hold a dumbbell in each hand with the palms facing forward.
Curl the weights up to shoulder height, keeping the upper arms perfectly still.
Squeeze hard at the top, then lower all the way to a dead stretch.

name: Dumbbell Concentration Curl
description: Bracing the elbow against the thigh removes every other muscle from the equation.
instructions: Sit on a bench with the legs spread and lean forward over one thigh.
Brace the back of your working upper arm against the inside of that thigh.
Curl the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, squeezing hard at the top.
Lower slowly to full extension before the next rep.

name: Zottman Curl
description: Curl up palms-up, lower palms-down: one rep trains the biceps and the forearms separately.
instructions: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing forward.
Curl both weights up to shoulder height as you would a normal curl.
At the top, rotate the palms to face down.
Lower slowly in that overhand position, then rotate back to palms-up at the bottom.

name: Dumbbell Hammer Curl To Front Press
description: A curl and press in one rep, so the arms and shoulders share the work with no rest between.
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing in.
Hammer curl both dumbbells up to shoulder height.
From there, press them straight overhead without rotating the wrists.
Lower back to the shoulders, then down to the start to complete the rep.

name: Standing Cable Curl
description: Cables keep the biceps loaded at the bottom of the rep, where dumbbells go slack.
instructions: Set two low pulleys and take a handle in each hand, standing between them.
Raise the arms out to the sides at shoulder height with the palms facing up.
Curl both hands in toward your ears, keeping the upper arms level.
Extend the arms back out slowly against the cable tension.

name: Floor Cable Curl
description: Lying on the floor pins the upper arms in place, making this a great starter or finisher.
instructions: Attach a bar to a low pulley and lie on the floor with your feet toward the machine.
Hold the bar with an underhand grip and the arms extended toward the pulley.
Curl the bar toward your forehead, keeping the elbows planted on the floor.
Extend the arms back out slowly, never letting the stack touch down.

name: Rope Hammer Curl
description: A neutral-grip cable curl with constant tension on the brachialis from bottom to top.
instructions: Attach a rope to a low pulley and hold an end in each hand, palms facing each other.
Stand tall with the elbows pinned to your sides.
Curl the rope up to chest height, pulling the ends slightly apart at the top.
Lower under control to full extension.

name: Outside-Grip Rope Curl
description: Gripping the outside of the rope widens the hands and shifts work to the short head.
instructions: Attach a rope low and take hold of the outer edges with the palms facing up.
Stand tall with the elbows tucked in and the shoulders down.
Curl up to chest height, keeping the hands wide the whole way.
Lower slowly against the cable to a full stretch.

name: Inside-Grip Rope Curl
description: A narrow rope grip that emphasises the long head and lets you squeeze hard at the top.
instructions: Take the rope with the hands close together, palms facing up.
Keep the elbows locked to your sides and stand tall.
Curl the rope up toward your chin and hold the contraction for a beat.
Extend the arms back down slowly under tension.

name: Cable EZ-Bar Curl
description: Combines the wrist-friendly EZ-bar angle with the constant tension of a cable.
instructions: Clip an EZ attachment to a low pulley and take the outer grips, palms up.
Step back until the cable is taut and stand tall with the elbows at your sides.
Curl the bar to chest height without letting the elbows travel forward.
Lower slowly to full arm extension against the resistance.

name: Biceps Curl Machine
description: A preacher-style machine curl that fixes the elbows so form cannot break down.
instructions: Set the seat so your armpits rest comfortably on the top of the pad.
Grip the handles with the palms up and the arms almost straight.
Curl the handles up until the biceps are fully contracted.
Lower under control to near-full extension without letting the plates rest.

name: Cable Bicep Punch
description: An alternating cable curl performed from a staggered stance for a longer, sweeping range.
instructions: Set two low pulleys and take a handle in each hand with a staggered stance.
Start with both arms extended down and slightly behind you.
Curl one arm up in a punching arc toward the opposite shoulder.
Return under control and alternate arms throughout the set.

name: Cable Bicep Kiss
description: A high-cable curl where the hands finish beside the head, giving a hard peak contraction.
instructions: Set both pulleys at head height and take a handle in each hand, palms up.
Stand in the middle with the arms extended out to the sides.
Curl both hands in toward your ears without dropping the elbows.
Squeeze at the top, then extend the arms back out slowly.

name: Bicep Contractions
description: A self-resisted isometric drill for finishing off the biceps with no equipment at all.
instructions: Bend one arm to 90 degrees and press the opposite hand down against that wrist.
Curl against your own resistance, letting the arm move slowly upward.
Hold the peak contraction and squeeze as hard as you can for a few seconds.
Lower slowly against resistance and repeat, then swap arms.

name: Close-Grip Bench Press
description: The heaviest triceps exercise there is, and the fastest way to add pounds to your bench.
instructions: Lie on the bench and take a grip about shoulder-width -- narrower than that hurts the wrists.
Unrack the bar and set it over your lower chest with the shoulder blades pinned.
Lower the bar to the bottom of your sternum, keeping the elbows tucked close to your ribs.
Press back up by driving through the triceps until the arms lock out.

name: EZ-Bar Skull Crusher
description: The classic triceps mass builder, loading all three heads through a deep stretch.
instructions: Lie flat holding an EZ-bar over your chest with a close overhand grip.
Set the arms at a slight backward angle rather than straight up -- this keeps tension on the triceps.
Bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead or just behind your head.
Extend back to the start without letting the upper arms drift forward.

name: Dumbbell Skull Crusher
description: Dumbbells let each arm find its own path, which is usually kinder on the elbows than a bar.
instructions: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand held over your chest, palms facing each other.
Angle the arms slightly back toward your head to load the long head.
Bend the elbows and lower the dumbbells beside your ears.
Extend the arms back to the start, keeping the upper arms locked in place.

name: Tate Press
description: A powerlifting accessory that hammers the triceps lockout without stressing the elbows.
instructions: Lie flat with the dumbbells held over your chest, palms facing forward.
Lower the weights by flaring the elbows out and bringing the dumbbells down to your chest.
The dumbbell heads should meet in the middle at the bottom of the rep.
Press back up by extending the elbows, squeezing the triceps hard at lockout.

name: Pull-Over And Press
description: A skull crusher joined to a pull-over, giving the long head of the triceps a far longer stretch.
instructions: Lie flat with an EZ-bar held over your chest with a close grip.
Bend the elbows to lower the bar behind your head like a skull crusher.
From there, keep the arms bent and pull the bar back over your face in an arc.
Press the bar out to lockout over your chest to finish the rep.

name: Overhead Triceps Extension
description: Taking the arms overhead puts the long head under a deep stretch, which is where it grows.
instructions: Hold a single dumbbell with both hands and press it straight overhead.
Brace the core and squeeze the glutes so the lower back does not arch.
Lower the weight behind your head by bending at the elbows only.
Extend back to lockout, keeping the upper arms pointing at the ceiling throughout.

name: Standing EZ-Bar Overhead Extension
description: A standing overhead extension that also demands real core bracing to stay upright.
instructions: Take a close overhand grip on an EZ-bar and press it overhead.
Stand tall with the feet hip-width, glutes squeezed and ribs pulled down.
Lower the bar behind your head under control until you feel a deep triceps stretch.
Extend back overhead without letting the elbows flare wide apart.

name: Seated EZ-Bar Overhead Extension
description: Sitting with back support removes the balance element so you can push the triceps harder.
instructions: Sit on an upright bench and press an EZ-bar overhead with a close grip.
Keep the back flat against the pad and the elbows pointing forward.
Lower the bar behind your head slowly to a full stretch.
Press back to lockout, keeping the upper arms as still as possible.

name: Seated Dumbbell Overhead Extension
description: A supported two-handed overhead extension -- a simple, reliable long-head builder.
instructions: Sit on an upright bench and hold one dumbbell overhead with both hands cupping the top plate.
Press your back into the pad and keep the elbows tight and pointing forward.
Lower the dumbbell behind your head until the forearms touch the biceps.
Extend back overhead and squeeze the triceps at the top.

name: Single-Arm Overhead Extension
description: One arm at a time, so a weaker side cannot hide behind the stronger one.
instructions: Press a dumbbell overhead in one hand with the palm facing forward.
Support the working elbow with your free hand to keep it from drifting.
Lower the weight behind your head until you feel a strong stretch.
Extend back to lockout, then complete the set before switching arms.

name: Lying Dumbbell Triceps Extension
description: A lying extension where the dumbbells travel past the head for extra range of motion.
instructions: Lie flat holding a dumbbell in each hand over your chest, palms facing each other.
Tilt the arms back slightly so the weights sit over your forehead.
Bend the elbows and lower the dumbbells past your ears toward the bench.
Extend back up without letting the upper arms swing forward.

name: Dumbbell Triceps Press
description: A close, neutral-grip press that shifts most of the bench press load onto the triceps.
instructions: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other and weights touching.
Keep the dumbbells pressed together throughout the set.
Lower them to your lower chest with the elbows tucked tight to your ribs.
Press straight back up to lockout, squeezing the triceps at the top.

name: Dumbbell Triceps Kickback
description: An isolation move that peaks at full lockout, where the triceps are shortest.
instructions: Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back, dumbbell in hand.
Pin the upper arm against your side so it is parallel to the floor.
Extend the elbow to straighten the arm behind you.
Squeeze for a beat at lockout, then bend the elbow back to 90 degrees.

name: Cable Triceps Pushdown
description: The most-used triceps exercise in any gym, and the easiest to load progressively.
instructions: Attach a straight or angled bar to a high pulley and grip it overhand at shoulder-width.
Stand close to the machine with the elbows pinned to your sides and a slight forward lean.
Push the bar down until the arms are fully locked out.
Let the bar rise back to chest height without letting the elbows travel forward.

name: Rope Triceps Pushdown
description: The rope lets the hands split apart at the bottom for a harder peak contraction than a bar.
instructions: Attach a rope to a high pulley and hold an end in each hand, palms facing each other.
Tuck the elbows to your sides and lean forward slightly.
Push down and pull the rope ends apart as the arms lock out.
Return under control to chest height, keeping the upper arms still.

name: Cable Triceps Lunge Extension
description: An overhead cable extension from a lunge stance, adding a core and hip stability demand.
instructions: Set a rope on a low pulley, face away from the machine and take it overhead.
Step into a split stance with the torso upright and the core braced.
Extend the arms forward and up until they lock out over your head.
Bend the elbows to lower the rope behind your head under control.

name: Triceps Extension Machine
description: A plate-loaded extension that fixes the elbow position so the triceps do all the work.
instructions: Set the seat so your elbows rest on the pad in line with the machine pivot.
Grip the handles and start with the arms bent.
Extend the arms fully, pushing the handles down and away.
Return slowly to the stretched position without letting the weight rest.

name: Arm Extension Machine
description: A seated selectorised triceps machine -- a straightforward starting point for beginners.
instructions: Adjust the seat so your upper arms lie flat on the pad.
Grip the handles with the elbows bent to about 90 degrees.
Press down and forward until the arms are straight.
Let the handles return slowly to the start position.

name: Triceps Dip
description: The same dip as the chest version, but staying upright turns it into a triceps movement.
instructions: Support yourself on parallel bars with the arms locked and the shoulders pressed down.
Keep the torso as vertical as you can -- this is what shifts the load to the triceps.
Lower with the elbows tracking straight back until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press back up to a hard lockout without leaning forward.

name: Bench Dip
description: A scalable triceps dip using a bench -- move your feet out to make it harder.
instructions: Sit on the edge of a bench and grip the edge beside your hips, then slide your hips off.
Extend the legs out in front, heels on the floor, arms locked out.
Lower by bending the elbows straight back until the upper arms are parallel to the floor.
Press back up to lockout, keeping the hips close to the bench.

name: Diamond Push-Up
description: A narrow push-up that shifts most of the load off the chest and onto the triceps.
instructions: Set your hands under your chest with the thumbs and index fingers forming a diamond.
Hold a rigid plank from heels to head with the glutes squeezed.
Lower your chest to your hands, keeping the elbows brushing your ribs.
Press back up to full lockout without letting the hips sag.

name: Triceps Contractions
description: A self-resisted isometric finisher for the triceps that needs nothing but your other arm.
instructions: Bend one arm and place the opposite hand against that wrist to provide resistance.
Push the working arm into extension against your own hand.
Hold the locked-out position and squeeze the triceps hard for several seconds.
Bend the arm back slowly against resistance, then repeat and swap sides.

name: Seated Barbell Wrist Curl
description: Direct work for the forearm flexors, the muscles on the inside of your arm that drive grip.
instructions: Sit on a bench with your forearms resting on your thighs, palms facing up.
Let the bar roll down to your fingertips so the wrists are fully extended.
Curl the bar back up by closing the fingers and flexing the wrists.
Squeeze at the top, then lower slowly back to the fingertips.

name: Seated Reverse Wrist Curl
description: Trains the extensors on the top of the forearm -- often the weak link behind elbow pain.
instructions: Sit with your forearms on your thighs and the bar held overhand, palms facing down.
Let the wrists drop as far as they comfortably go.
Raise the backs of the hands toward the ceiling by extending the wrists.
Hold the top for a beat, then lower under control. Use light weight.

name: Standing Wrist Curl
description: A wrist curl done standing with the bar behind your back, easy to slot in at the end of a session.
instructions: Stand holding a barbell behind your glutes with an overhand grip, arms straight.
Let the bar roll down into your fingers so the wrists extend.
Curl the bar up by closing the fingers and flexing the wrists.
Lower slowly back to the fingertip position.

name: Standing Reverse Wrist Curl
description: Standing extensor work for the top of the forearms, useful for elbow health.
instructions: Stand holding a bar in front of your thighs with an overhand grip.
Keep the arms straight and let the wrists hang down.
Raise the backs of your hands upward by extending the wrists only.
Lower under control and keep the weight light enough to avoid swinging.

name: Single-Handed Wrist Curl
description: One arm at a time, with the forearm braced so nothing else can contribute.
instructions: Kneel beside a bench and rest one forearm along it with the palm facing up.
Hold a dumbbell and let it roll down toward your fingertips.
Curl the weight up by flexing the wrist and closing the hand.
Lower slowly to full extension, then finish the set and switch arms.

name: Single-Handed Reverse Wrist Curl
description: Braced single-arm extensor work -- one of the best drills for stubborn elbow tendon issues.
instructions: Rest one forearm along a bench with the palm facing down and the hand hanging off the end.
Hold a light dumbbell and let the wrist drop fully.
Raise the back of the hand toward the ceiling by extending the wrist.
Pause at the top and lower slowly, then swap arms.

name: Forearm Twist
description: Trains rotation of the forearm, which flexion and extension work both miss.
instructions: Rest your forearm on a bench or thigh with the hand hanging off, holding a dumbbell by one end.
Start with the palm facing down and the weight held out horizontally.
Rotate the forearm to turn the palm all the way up.
Rotate back to palm-down under control -- go light and move slowly.

name: Farmers Walk
description: A loaded carry that builds grip, traps and full-body bracing all at once.
instructions: Pick up a heavy dumbbell or kettlebell in each hand with a flat back.
Stand tall with the shoulders pulled back and the core braced hard.
Walk in a straight line with short, controlled steps and the weights hanging at your sides.
Walk for distance or time, and set the weights down with a hinge rather than dropping them.

name: Barbell Front Squat
description: A quad-dominant squat that forces an upright torso and punishes any loss of position.
instructions: Rest the bar across your front delts with the elbows driven high and the fingers under the bar.
Unrack and set your feet shoulder-width with the toes turned out slightly.
Sit straight down between your hips, keeping the elbows up and the torso near vertical.
Drive up out of the bottom without letting the elbows drop -- that is what causes the bar to dump.

name: Zercher Squat
description: Holding the bar in the crooks of the elbows forces brutal upper-back and core engagement.
instructions: Set the bar around waist height and hook it into the crooks of your elbows.
Stand up with the bar held tight against your torso, hands clasped together.
Squat down between your knees, keeping the chest up and the elbows inside the thighs.
Drive back up through the whole foot -- use a pad or towel, the bar bites.

name: Jefferson Squat
description: A straddled squat with the bar between the legs, loading each side differently.
instructions: Straddle the bar with one foot in front and one behind, feet turned out.
Grip the bar with one hand in front of you and one behind, then set a flat back.
Stand up by driving the hips forward and extending the knees.
Lower back to the floor under control, then repeat and switch your stance for the next set.

name: Barbell Duck Walk
description: Walking in a deep squat under load -- a punishing drill that carries over to squats and deadlifts.
instructions: Rack a light bar on your back or hold it in a front-rack position.
Drop into a deep squat and stay there for the whole set.
Take small steps forward without letting the hips rise out of the squat.
Walk for a set distance, then stand up carefully and rack the bar.

name: Smith Machine Squat
description: The fixed bar path lets you push a squat close to failure safely without a spotter.
instructions: Set the bar on your upper traps and walk your feet slightly forward of the bar.
Rotate the bar to unhook it and brace the core.
Descend until the thighs are at least parallel, keeping the back flat against the bar path.
Drive back up through the heels and re-hook the bar at the end of the set.

name: Smith Machine Hack Squat
description: Feet forward and bar on the back -- the closest you can get to a hack squat machine on a Smith.
instructions: Set the bar on your traps and walk the feet well out in front of your hips.
Lean back against the bar path so the quads take the load.
Squat down deep, keeping the heels planted and the back supported.
Press back up through the whole foot without locking the knees hard at the top.

name: Seated Leg Press
description: Loads the legs heavily with no balance or lower-back demand -- ideal for high-volume quad work.
instructions: Sit with your back and hips flat against the pad and feet shoulder-width on the platform.
Release the safeties and lower the platform under control.
Stop when the knees reach about 90 degrees, or before the lower back rounds off the seat.
Press back out through the whole foot, stopping just short of locking the knees.

name: Single-Leg Press
description: One leg at a time on the press, which exposes and fixes side-to-side strength differences.
instructions: Place one foot in the centre of the platform with the other resting off to the side.
Keep your hips square and flat against the seat.
Lower the platform until the knee reaches about 90 degrees.
Press back out under control, then complete the set before switching legs.

name: Leg Extension
description: The only common exercise that isolates the quads with no hip involvement at all.
instructions: Set the seat so your knees line up with the machine pivot and the pad sits on your lower shins.
Sit back with the thighs flat and grip the handles to stop yourself lifting off.
Extend the knees until the legs are straight and squeeze the quads hard at the top.
Lower slowly under control rather than letting the stack drop.

name: Single-Leg Extension
description: Isolating one quad at a time gives a harder contraction and evens out imbalances.
instructions: Set the machine as for a normal leg extension but place only one shin behind the pad.
Sit back with the hips square and the working thigh flat on the seat.
Extend the knee to full lockout and hold the squeeze for a beat.
Lower slowly to the start, then finish the set before switching legs.

name: Barbell Reverse Lunge
description: Stepping backward is far easier on the knees than a forward lunge and loads the glutes harder.
instructions: Rack the bar on your upper back and stand with the feet hip-width apart.
Take a controlled step backward and lower the back knee toward the floor.
Keep the front shin roughly vertical and the torso upright.
Drive through the front heel to return to standing, then alternate legs.

name: Barbell Walking Lunge
description: A loaded walking lunge, one of the toughest leg-builders you can program.
instructions: Rack the bar across your upper back and brace hard before the first step.
Step forward and lower the back knee to just above the floor.
Drive through the front heel and step straight into the next lunge.
Keep the torso upright and the steps long enough that the front knee stays behind the toes.

name: Dumbbell Reverse Lunge
description: The most joint-friendly loaded lunge, and a good first single-leg exercise.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides and stand tall.
Step one foot back and lower the knee toward the floor under control.
Keep the weight in the front heel and the torso upright.
Push through the front leg to stand, then alternate sides.

name: Dumbbell Walking Lunge
description: A walking lunge with dumbbells -- easy to load progressively and easy to bail out of.
instructions: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with the chest tall.
Step forward into a lunge, lowering the back knee toward the floor.
Push off the front heel and bring the back leg through into the next step.
Keep the steps consistent and the torso from leaning forward as you fatigue.

name: Bodyweight Reverse Lunge
description: The unloaded version, and the right place to learn the pattern before adding weight.
instructions: Stand tall with the hands on your hips and the feet hip-width apart.
Step one leg back and lower the knee toward the floor.
Keep the front shin vertical and the chest up.
Drive through the front heel back to standing and alternate sides.

name: Bodyweight Stepping Lunge
description: A forward walking lunge with no load -- great as a warm-up or a conditioning finisher.
instructions: Stand tall with the hands on your hips or out for balance.
Step forward and lower until both knees are at roughly 90 degrees.
Push off the front heel and step through into the next rep.
Keep the torso upright and the steps controlled rather than rushed.

name: Bulgarian Split Squat
description: A rear-foot-elevated split squat -- brutally effective and unforgiving of poor balance.
instructions: Set the rear foot on a bench behind you and hop the front foot far enough forward.
Lower straight down until the rear knee is just off the floor.
Keep the front shin close to vertical and the torso slightly forward.
Drive through the front heel to stand, without pushing off the back foot.

name: Sissy Squat
description: A knee-flexion squat that stretches the quads under load like nothing else.
instructions: Hold a rack or door frame for balance and rise up onto the balls of your feet.
Push the knees forward and lean the torso back, keeping hips and shoulders in one line.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch through the front of the thighs.
Pull yourself back up using the quads. Build up slowly -- this is hard on the knees.

name: Pistol Squat
description: A full single-leg squat -- the benchmark for lower-body strength, balance and mobility combined.
instructions: Stand on one leg with the other extended straight out in front of you.
Reach the arms forward as a counterbalance and sit back and down slowly.
Descend as far as you can while keeping the heel flat on the floor.
Drive back up without letting the free leg touch down. Use a box or strap to regress it.

name: Single-Leg Box Squat
description: The main progression toward a pistol squat -- the box sets the depth and catches you.
instructions: Stand on one leg in front of a box or bench with the other leg extended forward.
Sit back and down under control until your glutes touch the box.
Do not relax onto it -- stay tight and pause for a beat.
Drive back up through the standing heel, then lower the box height as you get stronger.

name: Air Squat
description: The unloaded squat. Get this right and every loaded squat variation gets easier.
instructions: Stand with the feet shoulder-width and the toes turned out slightly.
Reach the arms forward for balance and push the hips back as you bend the knees.
Descend until the hip crease is below the knee, keeping the heels flat.
Drive up through the whole foot and squeeze the glutes at the top.

name: Bosu Ball Squat
description: Squatting on an unstable surface, which turns a leg exercise into a balance drill.
instructions: Step carefully onto the flat side of a Bosu ball with the feet shoulder-width apart.
Find your balance and brace the core before moving.
Squat down slowly, keeping the ball as level as you can.
Stand back up under control -- keep the reps slow, this is not a loading exercise.

name: Double Bosu Ball Lunge
description: A split squat with both feet on unstable surfaces -- a serious balance and stabiliser challenge.
instructions: Set two Bosu balls a stride apart and step onto them into a split stance.
Find your balance with the torso upright and the core braced hard.
Lower into the lunge slowly, keeping both balls level.
Press back up through the front leg without letting the knee wobble inward.

name: Wall Sit
